newsitem.title: USA: New official not sure he will prosecute Kevorkian.
newsitem.headline: New official not sure he will prosecute Kevorkian.

text.p: The man who will take over as top prosecutor of Michigan's Oakland County said Wednesday it was unlikely he would pursue common-law charges against assisted-suicide activist Dr. Jack Kevorkian.

David Gorcyca, calling the euthanasia controversy a "front-burner" issue for him, told Reuters he believed state lawmakers should deliberate and give the public a clear lead. "I'm looking for the legislature in Lansing to address that issue once and for all," he said.

Gorcyca added that he needed to review the common-law criminal charges of assisting in a suicide brought against Kevorkian last week before deciding whether to continue to press them when he took office in January.
"I'm not sure what steps I will take. I want to review each of the cases and look at the facts and the circumstances and take whatever necessary and appropriate actions I see fit," he said.

Gorcyca, a city commissioner for Detroit suburb Royal Oak and one-time assistant prosecutor, was originally believed to have lost Tuesday's race to succeed Richard Thompson as Oakland County's chief prosecutor. But an error was discovered Wednesday morning and Gorcyca was named the winner over Democrat Steve Kaplan by a count of 239,423 to 232,193.

Kevorkian has proven an elusive quarry for prosecutors. The fiery 68-year-old retired pathologist has been acquitted of criminal charges in three trials involving five deaths. Two of those trials occurred this year under Thompson, a conservative law-and-order prosecutor who has become a bitter enemy of Kevorkian and his lawyer, Geoffrey Fieger.

Last week Thompson's office lodged 19 new charges against Kevorkian involving 10 deaths he has attended since June. Kevorkian has admitted being present at 45 suicides since he began his crusade to legalise euthanasia in 1990.

Michigan lawmakers enacted a ban on physician-assisted suicide 3 years ago, except when it was meant to relieve pain and suffering. But the law expired in November 1994 and the legislature refused to renew it.
In December 1994 the Michigan Supreme Court ruled that assisted suicide was prohibited by the unwritten common law.

In addition to alleged common law violations, the most recent complaint includes charges not previously brought against Kevorkian such as removing dead bodies without permission of the medical examiner and representing himself as a practicing physician while engaged in an unlawful act.
